passage:
"Football again?" Kishore said. "Raghav, you're on my side."
"Okay," Raghav said, though he'd wanted to play carrom.
Later the ball smashed the staffroom window. "Who kicked it?" the PT sir asked.
Kishore went pale. Raghav stepped forward. "Me, sir."
After school Kishore caught up with him. "Why did you say that? It was my kick."
"You looked scared. I didn't want a fight."
"You hate football, don't you?"
Raghav shrugged. "Everyone was happy."
"I'd still be your friend if you said no, you know. Tomorrow, carrom?"
Raghav looked up. "Really?"
"Really. And I'm telling sir it was me."

qa.q: What had Raghav wanted to play instead?
Why did Raghav take the blame for the broken window?
qa.a: He felt Kishore was scared and wanted to avoid a fight; keeping everyone happy felt safer to him.

qa.q: What turning point came when Kishore caught up after school?
qa.a: Kishore said they would still be friends if Raghav said no and offered carrom, showing that refusing would not end the friendship.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel when Raghav took the blame for Kishore's kick?
qa.a: Kishore seems uncomfortable and guilty, which is why Kishore decides to tell sir the truth.

grounding: A boy agrees to games he dislikes and takes blame to avoid conflict, and his friend shows him that saying no won't break their friendship.

passage:
Last year I was the one who always said, "I don't mind." If Gargi wanted to play house, I played house, even though I wanted to draw. When our group fought over who spilled ink on the class chart, I said it was me, just so the shouting would stop. It wasn't me. I felt calm for about a minute, and then heavy for the whole day. One evening I told my Masi about the ink, and she said, "A friend who leaves because you said no was never really your friend." The next week, when Gargi said house again, I said, "Can we draw first?" She blinked, then said, "Okay, draw first." Nothing broke.
Hansa

qa.q: What did Hansa want to do instead of playing house?
How did Hansa feel after taking the blame for the ink?
qa.a: Hansa felt calm for about a minute and then heavy for the whole day.

qa.q: What choice did Hansa make the next week, and what happened?
qa.a: Hansa asked to draw first, and Gargi simply agreed, so nothing broke.

qa.q: What might Gargi have thought when Hansa finally asked to draw first?
qa.a: She was a little surprised, but happy to go along, which shows she cared more about the friendship than the game.

grounding: A child who always agreed and even took blame to keep the peace learns, with an aunt's help, that saying no does not break a friendship.
